This is a fresh three-node GNS3 project inside the existing VMware-hosted GNS3 VM. Setup is an instructor-assisted prerequisite, separate from the numbered lessons. Lessons 1–3 can be studied in guided-analysis mode while runtime is gated. They teach decisions, then addressing, then services; detailed policy administration remains later in the 36-lesson course.

Stop before changing an appliance

  1. Record exact version/build, valid/invalid license status and supported CPU/RAM/interfaces. Do not share the full status output. Check available host/GNS3 memory and KVM support; historical 16 GB host / 2 GB GNS3 values are unverified. Do not change allocations or host security.
  2. Use an entitled appliance workflow without cloning licensed disks, moving assignments, upgrading firmware or activating another instance. If a new instance needs activation or resources, stop for a separate authorized preflight. Preserve old projects.
  3. Create a blank project named QCS-FortiGate-Foundations; use the existing approved template only when license use is settled. Add disposable Ubuntu client/server with iproute2, curl and Python 3 already installed through an authorized provisioning process. No package download is needed in the isolated exercise.
  4. Connect client data NIC to verified FortiGate client port, and server NIC to verified server port. Leave management disconnected initially. No Cloud, NAT, bridge, shared DHCP or links to other projects. Outer VM NAT is not proof of guest isolation.
  5. Verify NIC/MAC/cable mappings using console interface listings and GNS3 adapter records. Port2/port3 in this pack are provisional. If ranges overlap, revise manifest, commands and all visuals together before use.

Console versus GUI

Right-click the intended GNS3 node → Console opens its text terminal. FortiGate’s top-level prompt resembles hostname #; Ubuntu resembles user@LabClient:~$. These prompts identify where to type and are never copied. A GUI is a browser dashboard and needs a separately verified private management route. A Linux sudo prompt asks for the local password privately; typed characters may be invisible.

At the FortiGate top-level prompt, get system status reads system metadata; privately retain only version/build and license-validity summary. show system interface reads configured interface names and addresses. These may reveal identifiers: inspect locally, never upload full output. If the prompt contains a configuration section, stop and return to top level with end before a read command.

Private management and baseline gate

Management subnet/address remain deliberately unassigned. Verify a dedicated host-only path, overlap checks, adapter binding and absence of physical uplinks before connecting port1. Use console access until that path is approved. Limit HTTPS administration to that private interface and the administrator host; do not enable it on the data ports. Verify certificate identity privately; do not blindly bypass certificate warnings.

Before any exercise change, obtain a protected baseline from the actual build. The 8.0 reference GUI path is username menu → Configuration → Backup → Local PC → FortiOS format → Encryption enabled. Keep the recovery password privately, verify the file exists and record its hash outside this served folder. A password-masked sharing copy is not a recovery backup. If GUI/private management is unavailable, hold configuration work until a supported protected backup method is verified. Do not substitute insecure TFTP.

Prepared baseline contract — instructor gate

After exact-build review, configure the manifest’s addresses and only the two endpoint-specific remote routes. No default Internet route. Ordinary routed, single-VDOM lab; connected FortiGate routes to both /24s; NAT off. Map objects QCS_CLIENT = 10.77.10.10/32, QCS_SERVER = 10.77.20.10/32, custom service QCS_TCP8080 = TCP destination 8080. An unused verified policy ID (proposed 1101) permits only port2 → port3, these two objects, this service, always schedule, logging enabled. No other data forwarding rule. Verify policy order, storage/log-view capability and host firewall allowance narrowly for this client/port. Do not disable endpoint security. Actual IDs/names must be checked for collisions.

This is a baseline specification, not a paste-ready FortiGate setup script. Final appliance configuration and its inverse must be generated after the build and original configuration are known. Lessons use read-only observations or disposable-endpoint changes. Do not claim an executable FortiGate configuration has been validated.

Transfer and service preparation

Transfer the included fixed-response helper to the disposable server using an approved private file-transfer channel, before final isolation. Record its SHA-256 against checksums.json. Do not add a public connection just to transfer it. Use the server console to run it; client console remains separate. It binds only the server lab address, returns fixed text and serves no disk files.

Acceptance and rollback

  • Record address, route, cable and private-management evidence; verify no public/default route or physical bridge.
  • Obtain encrypted baseline, record host firewall and policy state, then prove a fresh client HTTP request reaches the local helper, with matching policy/session or log evidence.
  • Keep evidence and backups outside this preview folder. The learner worksheet contains only safe summaries.
  • For cleanup stop only the helper with Ctrl+C; restore the endpoint route fault exactly as lesson 2 describes. Instructor deletes only newly created QCS policy and objects in dependency order, restores original data-interface values and narrow endpoint firewall changes from the recorded change ledger. Never touch management as casual cleanup.
  • If exact original values or ownership are unknown, stop; do not guess cleanup. Full backup restore is a separate disruptive recovery step: matching appliance/build, private console, username → Configuration → Restore, protected file/password, confirm reboot, then verify management and baseline. No factory reset or global session clearing.

01 / What a firewall decides and why

Explore the packet flow — pause, replay or open full screen to inspect headers.

Foundations: guided analysis. Animations are authored examples, not captured appliance results. Practical exercises are conditional drafts: run them only after exact-build licensing, isolation, private management, protected backup and baseline acceptance checks pass. No FortiGate/GNS3 appliance runtime has been validated for this course.

One question: who may talk to the application?

A firewall controls traffic between networks. A packet is a small addressed unit of data. A policy is an access rule. A flow is related traffic between endpoints; a session is the firewall’s tracked conversation state. A port identifies a transport endpoint; lesson 3 explains it fully. A firewall permit is permission, not proof of delivery or safety.

Worked example: staff LabClient needs the local application on LabServer, TCP 8080. The intended rule names this client, this server, the incoming/outgoing interfaces and that service. New unmatched forwarded traffic is denied in this baseline. Replies matching the allowed session can return; a new server-initiated connection is a different decision. This resembles a guest list, but a guest list cannot tell whether the application is running.

Keep these terms beside the explorer

MAC address
A link-layer address of a network interface, including a virtual NIC. This pack uses symbolic names instead of inventing actual MAC values.
Broadcast
A frame addressed to all receivers on its local Ethernet segment. The ARP request shown here is a local broadcast; it is not routed into the other lab subnet.
Frame / packet / segment
Ethernet carries a local-link frame; IP carries an addressed packet inside it; TCP carries a segment inside IP. These names describe different protocol layers.
Ingress / egress
Ingress is where traffic enters a device; egress is where it leaves. Their interface names must match the real cable mapping.
Implicit denial
The unmatched forwarding decision when no configured permit applies in this specified baseline. It is not a conclusion drawn merely from a timeout.
Evidence correlation
Matching observations by time and flow identifiers so that a server response, request and policy/session record refer to the same test.

Build the idea: a decision has several separate conditions

Start with the business request: “This disposable client needs the local web application.” Convert that sentence into a narrow flow. Source means the sender of a packet; destination means its intended receiver. An interface is the named network connection used to enter or leave a device. The request enters FortiGate through the client-facing port and leaves toward the server. The reply reverses these endpoint roles.

Keep five questions separate: is the cable/interface usable; does a route select a valid next hop; can local neighbors resolve each other; does policy permit this flow; and is the application listening and responding? A failure in any one can prevent the user’s request from succeeding. The firewall does not create the server’s return route or start its application.

ObservationWhat it supportsWhat it cannot prove alone
A narrow permit existsConfigured intention for a particular flowThat a request matched it or reached the server
The client selected the expected routeThe local stack predicts the expected next hopThat a packet was delivered
The helper records a requestThe application received that requestWhich firewall rule permitted it without correlation
Client receives HTTP 200The application answered this requestEncryption, user identity or broad network health
The request times outNo complete response within the chosen limitWhere the failure happened

Read the headers as nested envelopes

An Ethernet frame carries data across one local link. Its MAC addresses name the local sender and next receiver. Inside it, an IP packet names the remote IP endpoints. Inside that, a TCP segment identifies transport endpoints using ports and flags. Finally, HTTP carries the application request. Ethernet is replaced at this routed firewall; the IP/port endpoints remain unchanged here because NAT is off. Checksums, options and byte layout are beyond this introductory excerpt.

In the explorer, C_MAC, FG_P2_MAC, FG_P3_MAC and S_MAC are symbolic names for the four data-interface MACs. They are deliberately not invented hexadecimal addresses. ARP asks for a local IP neighbor’s MAC; it is not a TCP or UDP message and has no transport ports. A cached neighbor entry may make a new ARP exchange unnecessary.

Worked decision

Request A: client 10.77.10.10, destination 10.77.20.10, TCP destination 8080, client-facing ingress and server-facing egress. In the specified baseline it matches the narrow permit. Request B is a new connection with TCP destination 22. It does not match that permit and has no other matching forwarding policy in this baseline. Predict a drop; do not call it an observed result until a real controlled test and matching evidence exist. The practical lab below deliberately stops the service instead—it teaches why identical user symptoms may have different causes.

Lab 01 in smaller checkpoints

See the conversation

Rule under examination

Source 10.77.10.10/32 → destination 10.77.20.10/32; incoming verified port2, outgoing verified port3; TCP destination 8080.

Decision branch: match

If the narrow permit matches a new request, FortiGate can forward it. Delivery still requires routes and a running listener.

Decision branch: no match

A different service does not match that permit. In the specified baseline, unmatched new forwarded traffic is denied. This is a prediction, not an observed deny test.

Reply branch

Server → port3 → port2 → client, if it matches the permitted session and the return path works.

Complete step reference — readable without JavaScript
1. Decide whether the server is local

Ethernet: No frame sent yet

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: Planned TCP: 49152 → 8080

Decision: Endpoint route lookup, before the firewall

Why: The destination is outside the client /24. Use the route via 10.77.10.1; do not ARP for the remote server.

Evidence: Client: ip route get 10.77.20.10; this predicts a path without sending a request.

2. Find the gateway on the client link

Ethernet: C_MAC → ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff

IP / ARP: ARP asks: who has 10.77.10.1?

Transport: ARP has no TCP/UDP ports

Decision: Local ARP broadcast; not a forwarded TCP session

Why: With an empty neighbor cache, the client first needs the gateway MAC. This broadcast stays on the client segment.

Evidence: Client: ip neigh show. A cached valid entry may mean no new ARP request appears.

3. Gateway answers the ARP request

Ethernet: FG_P2_MAC → C_MAC

IP / ARP: ARP reply: 10.77.10.1 is at FG_P2_MAC

Transport: ARP; no TCP flags

Decision: Gateway is the local link destination

Why: MAC names here are symbols, not captured addresses. Record actual MACs privately before comparing a real trace.

Evidence: An ARP reply proves local neighbor resolution, not permission to reach the application.

4. Send the new TCP SYN to FortiGate

Ethernet: C_MAC → FG_P2_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: TCP SYN; 49152 → 8080

Decision: Ingress: verified port2

Why: The Ethernet destination is the gateway; the IP destination remains the server. Port2 receives a forwarded flow, not a login to FortiGate.

Evidence: Compare client route, source IP and bounded curl start time; actual client port will vary.

5. Evaluate the new flow

Ethernet: Ingress Ethernet header terminates here

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: TCP SYN; 49152 → 8080

Decision: Find a route and matching narrow policy; record session state if permitted

Why: The rule must match incoming/outgoing interfaces, client /32, server /32, TCP 8080 and schedule. This is a logical teaching checklist, not FortiOS internal execution order.

Evidence: Instructor correlates policy ID/action and the same tuple/time. A configured permit alone is not runtime evidence.

6. Resolve the directly connected server

Ethernet: FG_P3_MAC → ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff

IP / ARP: ARP asks: who has 10.77.20.10?

Transport: ARP; no TCP/UDP ports

Decision: Server-side neighbor lookup if not cached

Why: The outgoing link needs a server MAC. FortiGate does not forward the client-side ARP broadcast into this segment.

Evidence: A cold server-side neighbor cache may cause this separate ARP exchange. Do not clear caches for this lesson.

7. Server answers on its own segment

Ethernet: S_MAC → FG_P3_MAC

IP / ARP: ARP reply: 10.77.20.10 is at S_MAC

Transport: ARP; no TCP flags

Decision: Local server-side resolution

Why: A usable neighbor entry permits frame construction. It does not prove a process listens on TCP 8080.

Evidence: Server listener check is separate: ss -ltn. Expected local address: 10.77.20.10:8080.

8. Forward the SYN to the server

Ethernet: FG_P3_MAC → S_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: TCP SYN; 49152 → 8080

Decision: Egress: verified port3; NAT off

Why: A new Ethernet header is used on the server link. IP source/destination and transport ports are unchanged in this lab.

Evidence: In a real filtered trace, compare ingress and egress IP/port tuples; collect only the authorized local test.

9. Return SYN-ACK to FortiGate

Ethernet: S_MAC → FG_P3_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.20.10 → 10.77.10.10

Transport: TCP SYN-ACK; 8080 → 49152

Decision: Server route to 10.77.10.0/24 via 10.77.20.1

Why: The server reply goes to its local gateway MAC. The client is remote; the server does not send an Ethernet frame directly across the router.

Evidence: Server: ip route get 10.77.10.10. No route/fallback means reply delivery can fail before FortiGate receives it.

10. Forward the matching reply to the client

Ethernet: FG_P2_MAC → C_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.20.10 → 10.77.10.10

Transport: TCP SYN-ACK; 8080 → 49152

Decision: Match allowed session and usable return path

Why: This is a reply to the initiated session. A new server-initiated connection is a different policy decision.

Evidence: Check the same reversed tuple, not just the shared service port. Session state does not repair endpoint routes.

11. Acknowledge connection setup

Ethernet: C_MAC → FG_P2_MAC; then FG_P3_MAC → S_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: TCP ACK; 49152 → 8080

Decision: Client → port2 → port3 → server

Why: The handshake can complete while the later application fails. HTTP request/response is a further observation, taught in lesson 3.

Evidence: TCP setup evidence is weaker than a successful HTTP response. No TLS or VPN is configured.

12. Stop a separate unmatched new SYN

Ethernet: C_MAC → FG_P2_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: NEW TCP SYN; 49153 → 22

Decision: No matching forwarding permit in this specified baseline → drop

Why: This new destination port does not match TCP 8080. The animation stops at FortiGate and depicts no server response or invented reject packet.

Evidence: This is a predicted decision only. The practical service-stop fault is a different failure and is never labelled a verified firewall drop.

Bounded diagnosis and practice

If the baseline fails: (1) confirm the helper is running, (2) inspect client/server routes as lesson 2 teaches, (3) ask the instructor for the matching policy/log observation. Stop without broadening rules. Practice: explain why a correct rule and a stopped service can coexist; write one permitted tuple; identify the missing evidence in “it timed out.” Suggested answers: rule ≠ listener; use the tuple above; missing route/listener/policy correlation.

Evidence and boundaries

Use the evidence worksheet. Write prediction before observation; record time, exact command, endpoints, policy ID if available and a redacted result. Leave actual-result cells blank until tested. Never paste passwords, license files, serials, full configurations or recovery backups into the preview.

Stop after one failed attempt and up to three focused checks. A timeout alone is inconclusive: service, route, host filtering or firewall policy may be responsible. Restore the stated fault before trying a different hypothesis.

More practice • explain before revealing the answer

Which header names the gateway on the client link?

Ethernet destination FG_P2_MAC. The IP destination is still 10.77.20.10.

Does ARP use TCP port 8080?

No. ARP is a local link-address resolution protocol with no TCP/UDP ports.

A SYN-ACK returned. Has the helper served HTTP 200 yet?

No. TCP setup and HTTP response are separate observations.

Why is a new server-initiated connection different from a reply?

It initiates a different session and needs its own applicable policy decision.

Why can stopping the helper mimic a blocked request?

The client may fail to receive a useful response, even while the network permit remains unchanged.

What should accompany a claimed rule match?

Matching time, source/destination IPs, protocol/ports and actual policy/session evidence, with limits recorded.

Check your understanding

1. What does a firewall rule describe?

2. A TCP 8080 request times out. What is proven?

3. Which scope matches our business need?

4. A reply matching an allowed stateful session needs what?

5. Does plain HTTP in this lab protect payload confidentiality?

6. Which is runtime evidence?

Addresses tell us where; routes tell us the next step

Prerequisite: lesson 1. An IP address identifies an interface in this exercise. A subnet is a group described by a network prefix. In a /24, the first 24 bits are network bits: 10.77.10.10/24 has subnet 10.77.10.0/24 and mask 255.255.255.0. It has usable host addresses .1 through .254; .0 is the network and .255 the broadcast address in this conventional subnet. Do not generalize that last-octet rule to every prefix.

A gateway is a router on the local subnet used to reach another network. A route selects a next hop for a destination prefix. The client sends the remote server’s packet via 10.77.10.1; the server replies via 10.77.20.1. The destination IP stays the remote endpoint; link-layer delivery uses the gateway on each local link. A default route is a fallback, not a requirement here.

Keep these terms beside the explorer

Prefix
The network part of an address, written with a bit count such as /24. Here /24 corresponds to mask 255.255.255.0.
Next hop
The local router or directly attached receiver selected for the next link. It is not automatically the final IP destination.
Connected route
A route associated with an attached, addressed interface. In this baseline FortiGate connects both /24 lab networks.
Neighbor cache
Stored mappings between local neighbor IP and link-layer address. A cached entry can avoid a new ARP exchange.
TTL
IPv4 Time To Live, a forwarding-lifetime field that decreases when a router forwards the packet. No actual starting value is assumed in this pack.
Return path
The route choices needed to carry a reply back to the initiating endpoint. It must work in addition to the forward path.

Build the idea: subnet arithmetic without guessing

An IPv4 address has 32 bits, written here as four decimal octets. The prefix /24 says that 24 bits identify the network. The mask is 255.255.255.0. For this example, 10.77.10.10/24 belongs to 10.77.10.0/24; 10.77.20.10/24 belongs to 10.77.20.0/24. These are different networks. The “first three octets” shortcut is specific to /24; it is not a rule for every prefix.

A route describes where to send traffic for a destination prefix. The client’s route for 10.77.20.0/24 selects gateway 10.77.10.1. That gateway must itself be reachable on the client link. A default route is a fallback for destinations without a more specific match; the experiment needs no Internet default route. If overlapping routes exist, selection requires further checks; the beginner baseline deliberately avoids that complexity.

Two addresses answer different questions

Client frame: C_MAC → FG_P2_MAC answers “who receives this local Ethernet frame next?” Inside it, IP 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10 answers “which endpoints are communicating?” On the server link, the frame becomes FG_P3_MAC → S_MAC. The IP pair does not become a pair of firewall interface addresses. With ordinary IPv4 routing, TTL decreases as the packet is forwarded; no initial TTL or captured numeric value is assumed here.

On the reply, server IP 10.77.20.10 → client IP 10.77.10.10 travels first inside S_MAC → FG_P3_MAC, then FG_P2_MAC → C_MAC. A permitted session cannot repair a missing route on the server. This is why both directions appear in every acceptance check.

Worked failure analysis

Suppose the request can arrive, but the server’s only route to 10.77.10.0/24 is removed and there is no fallback. The server cannot select the intended remote reply path. The client may wait without a useful response. The decisive lesson evidence is the narrow route change plus the server route lookup and successful restoration—not the timeout alone.

No. It is the next local link receiver; the remote destination IP remains the server.

S_MAC → FG_P3_MAC, then FG_P2_MAC → C_MAC.

To verify ownership and capture the exact original prefix, next hop, NIC and any extra attributes.

Do not assume the fault was introduced; inspect the table and do not add a duplicate inverse.

No. It predicts local routing selection; the application request and response are separate evidence.

One address can host several services

Prerequisites: lessons 1–2. TCP provides an ordered byte stream using connection state, acknowledgements and retransmission; it cannot promise the application will succeed. UDP sends datagrams without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees. A socket endpoint combines an IP address, transport and port. A client usually uses a temporary ephemeral port; the server listens on a configured service port.

Worked example: illustrative client 10.77.10.10:49152 → server 10.77.20.10:8080 over TCP. Actual client ports vary. Reply: 10.77.20.10:8080 → 10.77.10.10:49152. Port 8080 is chosen for this helper; it does not prove application identity. DNS resolves names into records such as addresses, commonly using UDP or TCP 53. A name-based application may need both DNS access and application access. This lab has no DNS server.

Keep these terms beside the explorer

Socket endpoint
An IP address, transport protocol and port used by a communicating application. TCP 8080 and UDP 8080 are different transport endpoints.
Ephemeral port
A temporary client port chosen by the local stack. The illustrated 49152 is an example, not a runtime requirement.
Listener
A process waiting for traffic on a local address/transport/port. ss -ltn reads numeric listening TCP sockets.
SYN / ACK
TCP flags used in connection setup and acknowledgement. The three-message handshake is SYN, SYN-ACK, then ACK.
DNS A record
A DNS record supplying an IPv4 address for a name. An answer alone does not prove application access.
HTTP status
An application response code such as 200 or 404. Receiving an HTTP error is different from failing to establish any useful response.

Build the idea: transport setup, application data and naming

The address chooses an interface destination; the transport protocol and port choose a communication endpoint there. TCP port 8080 and UDP port 8080 are different transport endpoints. A server process must bind/listen on the address and transport expected by the client. A temporary client port lets the stack distinguish conversations; 49152 in these examples is a teaching value, not a promised runtime port.

Read the TCP handshake as three messages: SYN starts connection setup; SYN-ACK answers that setup from the server; ACK acknowledges it from the client. Afterward, HTTP request bytes can travel inside TCP. TCP supplies an ordered byte stream, so an HTTP message may span several segments or share a segment with other bytes; the illustrations do not assert packet-for-message boundaries.

What DNS adds—and what this lab deliberately supplies locally

A name such as app.qcs.test needs an address selection mechanism before the application can connect. A DNS A record can supply an IPv4 address. DNS is a separate conversation, commonly using UDP or TCP destination 53. A successful lookup does not permit the later HTTP flow. Conversely, an HTTP request to a numeric address does not require a lookup for that address.

The resolver in the explorer is an abstract dependency, with no assigned address, cable or configured GNS3 node. The actual exercise uses a numeric URL and then curl --resolve. The latter supplies a name/address mapping for that one curl invocation; it does not alter the system resolver or send a live query for that supplied mapping. Keep that distinction in the evidence worksheet.

HTTP status is another layer of evidence

HTTP 200 means the server answered the request successfully at the application layer. HTTP 404 from the included helper means it answered but did not serve that requested path. A connection refusal, timeout and HTTP error are different observations. None should automatically be renamed “FortiGate blocked it.” Plain HTTP does not encrypt the request or response.

Ethernet: S_MAC → FG_P3_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.20.10 → 10.77.10.10

Transport: TCP SYN + ACK; 8080 → 49152

Decision: Server has listener and return route

Why: SYN-ACK both acknowledges connection setup and supplies the server side of the handshake. It is not an HTTP response.

Evidence: A refused connection or reset differs from silence; neither alone identifies a FortiGate policy decision.

7. Firewall forwards the matching SYN-ACK

Ethernet: FG_P2_MAC → C_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.20.10 → 10.77.10.10

Transport: TCP SYN + ACK; 8080 → 49152

Decision: Reply matches the permitted conversation

Why: The reply source port is the server service port. The reply destination port is the client temporary port.

Evidence: Reverse both endpoint roles; do not mistakenly keep destination port 8080 in the reply.

8. Client completes setup with ACK

Ethernet: C_MAC → FG_P2_MAC; then FG_P3_MAC → S_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: TCP ACK; 49152 → 8080

Decision: TCP connection setup complete

Why: The handshake establishes transport state. It does not certify user identity, encrypt payloads or guarantee a useful application response.

Evidence: Sequence numbers, options, windows and most acknowledgements are omitted; no exact packet byte layout is claimed.

9. Send the HTTP request bytes

Ethernet: C_MAC → FG_P2_MAC; then FG_P3_MAC → S_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: TCP carrying HTTP GET /; 49152 → 8080

Decision: Request the helper root path /

Why: HTTP is the application protocol inside TCP. One application message is not guaranteed to equal one captured TCP segment.

Evidence: Client curl --include shows response headers; it is not a packet capture or a TLS check.

10. Return HTTP status and fixed body

Ethernet: S_MAC → FG_P3_MAC; then FG_P2_MAC → C_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.20.10 → 10.77.10.10

Transport: TCP carrying HTTP 200; 8080 → 49152

Decision: Expected helper response, if the whole path works

Why: A 200 response is stronger application evidence than a completed handshake. Plain HTTP does not protect confidentiality.

Evidence: Match the bounded client request, helper request line and policy/session evidence at the same time.

11. Separate application status from connectivity

Ethernet: No new frame required for this explanation

IP / ARP: 10.77.20.10 → 10.77.10.10

Transport: HTTP status is application data

Decision: For example, a 404 can show the server answered a different path

Why: A response error and a network timeout are different observations. Check what URL/path was requested before changing network rules.

Evidence: The included helper intentionally rejects non-root paths; a 404 from it is not proof that TCP was blocked.

12. Isolate name selection with --resolve

Ethernet: C_MAC → FG_P2_MAC; then FG_P3_MAC → S_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.10.10 → 10.77.20.10

Transport: TCP 49152 → 8080; curl supplies name mapping

Decision: Use app.qcs.test:8080:10.77.20.10 in this one command

Why: The HTTP Host name can stay app.qcs.test while the destination IP is supplied locally. No DNS server is queried for this mapping.

Evidence: Correct mapping and numeric URL should reach the same helper. Neither result verifies DNS infrastructure.

13. Fault only the command-local mapping

Ethernet: No trusted next-hop outcome is assumed

IP / ARP: Incorrect mapped destination: 10.77.20.99

Transport: TCP destination 8080; one bounded attempt

Decision: Use .99 only after it is verified unused in the isolated project

Why: A failure to the wrong address is not a DNS-server outage or a proved firewall block. The server-specific permit does not match .99.

Evidence: Restore the mapping to .10; do not edit hosts/resolver files or add broader rules.

14. Retest and clean up only the helper

Ethernet: S_MAC → FG_P3_MAC; then FG_P2_MAC → C_MAC

IP / ARP: 10.77.20.10 → 10.77.10.10

Transport: Fresh HTTP 200 expected after correct mapping restored

Decision: Verify listener, correct address and bounded response

Why: Restore the original command, make one fresh request, then Ctrl+C only the foreground helper if finished. No persistent DNS change was made.

Evidence: Record expected versus observed separately. No packet trace, FortiOS build or successful appliance test is invented.

Practical 03 • separate listener, HTTP and naming

Conditional practical: complete the exact-build setup and baseline gates first. Until then, use this as guided analysis and leave observed results blank.

Start the helper in the server console. In a second server terminal inspect the listening socket. If GNS3 exposes only one console, use a supported second guest terminal or stop and ask the instructor; do not background unknown processes.

SERVER second Ubuntu terminal:
ss -ltn

CLIENT:
curl --noproxy "*" --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 --include http://10.77.20.10:8080/
curl --noproxy "*" --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 --include --resolve app.qcs.test:8080:10.77.20.10 http://app.qcs.test:8080/

ss inspects sockets; -l means listeners, -t TCP, -n numeric values. Expected listener: 10.77.20.10:8080. This command is read-only. --resolve supplies an in-command name/address mapping for curl only; it is not a DNS query and changes no hosts file.

  1. Record the listener and numeric HTTP result; expect 200 if baseline passes.
  2. Run the supplied mapping request. Expected same HTTP response; it isolates name selection without a DNS server.
  3. Bounded fault: change only the mapping in the command to app.qcs.test:8080:10.77.20.99, after verifying .99 is unused in this isolated project. Expect failure. This is a deliberately wrong local mapping, not proof of DNS filtering.
  4. Rollback: rerun the original mapping to .10. No persistent file was changed. Acceptance: correct listener and HTTP 200 return. Cleanup: Ctrl+C in helper terminal.

Diagnosis and practice

Check three things in order: listener address/port, literal-IP HTTP result, supplied mapping string. If numeric access fails, do not start changing DNS. Stop after these checks and restore the original command. UDP and real DNS remain guided-analysis activities: draw client → resolver:53 and then client → application:8080 as two separate conversations. Practice: reverse the worked tuple; explain why a successful --resolve request does not prove DNS works; name one reason an allowed port may still fail. Answers: server:8080 → client:49152; no resolver was queried; stopped listener or missing route.

Evidence and boundaries

Use the evidence worksheet. Write prediction before observation; record time, exact command, endpoints, policy ID if available and a redacted result. Leave actual-result cells blank until tested. Never paste passwords, license files, serials, full configurations or recovery backups into the preview.

Stop after one failed attempt and up to three focused checks. A timeout alone is inconclusive: service, route, host filtering or firewall policy may be responsible. Restore the stated fault before trying a different hypothesis.

More practice • explain before revealing the answer

Why can TCP setup succeed while an application fails?

TCP transport setup does not guarantee the application supplies the requested response.

What are the reply ports for client 49152 → server 8080?

Server source 8080 → client destination 49152.

What does a 404 from this helper tell you?

The application answered a path it does not serve; TCP was not simply blocked for that response.

Does --resolve verify a DNS policy?

No. It supplies a mapping locally to curl for that command.

Why not add a DNS server silently to this topology?

It would change nodes, routes, policy dependencies and setup requirements beyond this three-node exercise.

Can an allowed port prove application identity or encryption?

No. A port number does not establish either.
